content.question_text: What does it mean if a method is 'overloaded' in Java?

core_requirements: Overloading occurs when several methods have the exact same name but different parameters.
acceptable_variations: Multiple methods sharing a name but taking different arguments.

content.question_text: How does the Java compiler determine which version of an overloaded method to execute?

core_requirements: It matches the parameter types in the method declarations with the types of the arguments provided in the specific method call.
This process is called overloading resolution.
acceptable_variations: By looking at the argument types passed in and finding the matching method signature.

content.question_text: What two pieces of information make up the 'signature' of a method?

core_requirements: The name of the method.
The parameter types it accepts.

content.question_text: Is the return type of a method considered part of its signature? Because of this, what is illegal to do in Java?

core_requirements: No, the return type is not part of the signature.
It is illegal to have two methods with the same name and parameter types but different return types.
acceptable_variations: No. You cannot overload a method by only changing its return type.

content.question_text: What happens if you do not explicitly initialize an instance field inside a constructor?

core_requirements: It is automatically set to a default value.
Numbers are set to 0, booleans to false, and object references to null.
acceptable_variations: It gets a default value of 0, false, or null.

content.question_text: What is the crucial difference between an uninitialized instance field and an uninitialized local variable in a method?

core_requirements: An instance field is automatically initialized to a default value (0, false, null).
A local variable is not automatically initialized and must be explicitly set, otherwise it causes a compile-time error.
acceptable_variations: Fields get default values automatically; local variables do not and will throw an error.

content.question_text: Under what specific condition does the Java compiler provide a free, no-argument constructor for your class?

core_requirements: Only when you write a class with no constructors whatsoever.
acceptable_variations: If you provide zero constructors, it gives you a default one.

content.question_text: If you define a custom constructor with arguments, what happens if someone tries to instantiate your class using a no-argument constructor (e.g., `new ClassName()`) without you explicitly writing one?

core_requirements: It will result in an error / it is illegal.
Because supplying any custom constructor removes the free default constructor.
acceptable_variations: It will fail to compile because the default constructor is no longer provided.

content.question_text: If you explicitly assign a value to an instance field directly in the class definition (e.g., `private String name = "";`), when exactly is this assignment carried out?

core_requirements: It is carried out before the constructor executes.
acceptable_variations: Prior to the constructor body running.

content.question_text: If a constructor parameter variable has the exact same name as an instance field, it 'shadows' that field. How do you properly access the instance field inside that constructor?

core_requirements: By prefixing the field name with `this.` (e.g., `this.salary`).

content.question_text: How can you call one constructor from inside another constructor of the same class, and why might you do this?

core_requirements: You use the `this(...)` keyword with the appropriate arguments.
It is done to eliminate duplicate construction code.
acceptable_variations: Use this() to avoid writing the same initialization logic twice.

content.question_text: In Java (prior to Java 25), what is the strict restriction regarding where you can place a call to another constructor (the `this(...)` keyword)?

core_requirements: It must be the very first statement of the constructor body.
acceptable_variations: It has to be the first line of code.

content.question_text: Aside from setting a value in a constructor or assigning a value in the field declaration, what is the third mechanism Java provides to initialize instance fields?

core_requirements: An initialization block (arbitrary blocks of code inside the class declaration).

content.question_text: When an object is constructed, which executes first: the field initialization blocks/declarations, or the body of the constructor?

core_requirements: The field initializers and initialization blocks execute first.
The body of the constructor executes last.
acceptable_variations: Blocks run before the constructor body.

content.question_text: If a static field requires complex initialization logic (like a loop or generating a random number), what mechanism should you use to initialize it?

core_requirements: A static initialization block (a block tagged with the keyword `static`).

content.question_text: When exactly does static initialization (like evaluating static assignments and static initialization blocks) occur in a Java program?

core_requirements: It occurs when the class is first loaded.
